content.text: Chapters and ArticlesYou might find these chapters and articles relevant to this topic.4.02.2.6 Generation Z (1997–2012)Generation Z is the youngest generation of individuals in our society that we examine in this chapter. This generation consists of individuals born between 1997 and 2012 who are presently 25 years old and younger. Generation Z's only frame of reference is a digital dominant world, one in which technology has been with them from birth, and is present, always in-hand, literally at one's fingertips. Research on Generation Z shows that 95% of this generation owns or has access to a smartphone and almost all (97%) use the internet daily (Vogels et al., 2022). Generation Z is arguably dependent on technology and relies on the internet and the smartphone for a large portion of daily communication, news, education and societal interaction. In a recent survey approximately 94.3% of millennials had some sort of social media account, (Curtis et al., 2019). As a result, Gen Z is largely influenced by what they read online from bloggers and their peers on social media accounts. As Generation Z is still relatively young, limited research exists in the literature on their views of healthcare and interactions with healthcare providers. Gen Z's healthcare perspective is felt to be largely influenced by the COVID-19 pandemic as this occurred while this group was in their teenage years and early twenties, in high school and college, during the height of the pandemic. As such, this group has been directly impacted with school, work and life interruptions and dramatically witnessed healthcare front and center and its overall importance for maintenance of wellness and the consequence of illness on a myriad of activities and aspects of society. According to one study, Gen Z actually had the most confidence, among all generations, as to the healthcare system and its operation during the pandemic (Villa et al., 2020). During the pandemic GenZ relied primarily on the web and social media as their main source of information. This group has a tendency to demand complete transparency from healthcare providers, with particular concern regarding the costs of healthcare (Wells et al., 2018). Further, evidence supports that this generation has an increased focus on mental health aspects of medicine, as well as the interplay of health and medicine with psychosocial issues. Of all the generations discussed so far it is Gen Z that is most likely to rely on and be impacted by Social Media now and well into the future as this means of communication and information sharing continues to evolve.Read full chapterURL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B97801282401060007214.02.2 The generations of todayWith a total of 333 million people in the United States, with an average lifespan of 77 years (Murphy et al., 2021; United States Census Bureau, 2022), the U.S. has an overall population that spans many “Generations.” In conventional parlance, a generation has multiple meanings, i.e., biological, social, political and economic. In this chapter we focus on social generations; defined as a group of individuals born and living contemporaneously, sharing similar ideas, attitudes and beliefs (Merriam-Webster, 2023). The concept of belonging to a social generation was originally proposed in the mid-1800s, by Auguste Comte describing social progress as “the product of generational change” in his work Cours de Philosophie Positive (Comte, 1830–1840; National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, 2020). The concept of social generations evolved throughout the nineteenth century, but it was not until 1952, that modern-day usage and understanding of social generations came into being (National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, 2020). Underlying this view of social generations is the work of sociologist Karl Mannheim, first detailed in his work, The Problem of Generations (1952). Mannheim (1952) proposed that a generation is a social phenomenon that links individuals based on historical-social processes. Since that time, the concept of social generations is increasingly recognized and utilized in modern society. It is now generally accepted that there is a fair to large degree of similarity of operational practice, values, interests, educational levels and occupational trajectories within a given generation; with much larger differences emerging between generations (Doherty et al., 2015; Dimock, 2019; Freeman, 2019).So the question is, why is defining generations important in the first place? At a minimum defining generations allows us to understand and compare individuals that make up our society chronologically—categorizing individuals based on the year and era in which they were born, and ontogenetically—by their current place in the human life cycle (infancy, adolescence, adulthood, and elderhood). More importantly, generational definition allows us to understand the context of that generation, i.e., how a particular population cohort has been influenced by events external to them, i.e., externalities. Being that all individuals are influenced by their backgrounds, their surrounding environments and the society in which they developed, people of differing generations necessarily have differing perspectives. As every aspect of our society—education, occupations, socioeconomic status racial and cultural bias, politics, environmental affairs and beyond continues to change, each generation has in turn been affected, and to a degree “imprinted,” by the collection of these events and circumstances. Hence, to delve into and understand generational behavior as to health, response to disease, attitudes to care, prevention and interaction with the healthcare system, it is only through understanding of the impact and sum of these externalities on each social generation, that we will then be able to understand and compare how individuals within a generation, i.e., intra-generation, versus between generations, i.e., inter-generational, behave and respond to the healthcare system as it evolves.We now discuss each social generation that currently makes up the U.S. population; defining their age group, beliefs, and values, to better understand their role in society.4.02.2.1 The Greatest Generation (1901–1927)—“The G.I. Generation”The Greatest Generation, also commonly known as the “Traditionalists,” consists of individuals born between 1901 and 1927 (White, 2022). Presently these individuals are elders between the ages of 95 and 121 years old. Traditionalists are touted for their sacrifice, humility, and patriotism, as they witnessed some of the most transformative events in American history (Ensign, 2020; White, 2022; Pumphrey, 2011). For this generation, technological advance, was initially much slower than today, largely driven by wartime influences of the first and second World Wars and was advanced in the spirit of patriotism. For the bulk of this generation, it was the radio and automobile that were the most widespread and popular technologies recognized during their upbringing. The Greatest Generation is known to be a civic-minded generation, focusing on a strong work ethic, family and religion. Higher education was not very common for this group, as people's options for schooling were often limited by socioeconomic status, race and gender. Similarly, medical education was also much more limited. The understanding of disease mechanisms, diagnosis and therapy were meager compared to today. This was certainly true of laymen. This generation suffered from a high mortality rate secondary to infectious diseases, as there was a lack of knowledge regarding hygiene and sanitation, this being the pre-antibiotic era, with limited therapeutic options, though this did start improving annually (Armstrong et al., 1999; CDC, 1999). Medical practices and hospitals were largely unregulated and individuals would often have to seek out physicians for in-home care, i.e., the housecall, which was only possible if they had the financial means to pay for these services. Thus, healthcare was not a primary focus of the Greatest Generation as the advances in the scientific underpinning of medicine lay ahead.4.02.2.2 The Silent Generation (1928–1945)The Silent Generation consists of individuals born between 1928 and 1945. These individuals are presently between 77 and 94 years old. The Silent Generation was particularly subject to social externalities and strain—being raised during a period of war and economic hardship, as they grew up during the Great Depression and/or World War II (WWII). Although times were difficult in the U.S. during these years, the individuals of this generation are well recognized for their innovative and entrepreneurial spirit and achievements. Advances for this group were largely due to the innovation frenzy following WWII, for which some of the greatest developments such as the emergence of antibiotics—penicillin and tetracyclines; and industrial materials, such as synthetic rubber and plastics emerged (Little, 2021). The most notable new home technology that was widely adopted by this generation was the refrigerator, and by 1931, near 15% of Americans had one in their home. Education was still fairly limited for the average U.S. citizen, though it was at a tipping point post-WWII with the passage of the GI Bill in 1944 providing stipends for tuition and expenses for veterans to attend college or trade schools (GI Bill—Servicemen’s Readjustment Act of 1944). Notably, there was a rise in research in both science and technology, driven through government funding sparked by the demands of war. Through this research, and the subsequent dissemination of discoveries, many individuals of the Silent Generation were able to obtain a greater understanding of science, health and medicine. Adoption of advances led to a greater average lifespan and an overall improvement in their health compared to the prior generation. As a result, this cohort generally trusts the opinions of their physicians regarding their healthcare needs, and is more likely to embrace their opinions for guidance on healthcare decisions (Integrated Healthcare Executive, 2016). Surprisingly, while the Silent Generation has the least technological experience with new devices, they are significant utilizers of digital healthcare portals for health maintenance and interactions with their physicians (Integrated Healthcare Executive, 2016).4.02.2.3 Baby Boomers (1946–1964)Baby Boomers are individuals born between 1946 and 1964, currently ranging from 58 to 76 years old. This generation grew up in the immediate post-war era, as the American economy was rapidly growing, i.e., “booming,” post-WWII. It was a period of growing social consciousness with the dawn of the Civil Rights Movement. As a result Baby Boomers are generally recognized as hard-workers, striving to make a good life for themselves their families being community conscious, and more economically prosperous than prior generations (Keister and Deeb-Sossa, 2004). This group has generally worked hard so as to be able to buy homes, cars and other consumer goods, including the latest technologies. These individuals were the trailblazers in introducing digital technology into their daily lives through the incorporation of radios, televisions, and home computers, paving the way for subsequent generations (Dholakia, 2012. During this time, technology was driven by the market and related demand (Dholakia, 2012). Education became more prominent and available, and more people crowded the classrooms (Keister and Deeb-Sossa, 2004). Science and technology became of increasing value, the pace of research accelerated and major advancements were made in medicine and the overall healthcare system. While health insurance was introduced into American society in the 1930s, it was not widely accepted until the era of the Baby Boomers, with approximately 71% of U.S. citizens covered by health insurance by the beginning of the 1960s, a rise from 50% at the beginning of 1950 (History.com Editors, 2022). Obtaining health insurance became essential as the average life expectancy of individuals increased. With this increase in life expectancy came an increase in the prevalence of “diseases of age,” including heart disease, stroke, and cancer (King et al., 2013). Baby Boomers are recognized as being extremely engaged in their healthcare and the healthcare needs of their parents and children (Integrated Healthcare Executive, 2016). While the Baby Boomers are less likely to smoke, and have lower rates of COPD/emphysema, they do tend to have higher rates of other chronic diseases and obesity (King et al., 2013). This cohort is also likely to conduct their own research on healthcare matters and engage in shared decision making with their healthcare providers, though with relative confidence in their physician's direction (Integrated Healthcare Executive, 2016). However, because Baby Boomers must manage the healthcare of multiple generations, it is recognized that they often receive multiple forms of input and utilize a range of communication means (verbal, written, and technological) to ensure their understanding (Integrated Healthcare Executive, 2016).4.02.2.4 Generation X (1965–1980)Generation X consists of people born between the years of 1965 and 1980. These individuals are presently 42–57 years old. This generation was raised during a period of immense globalization, as technological advancements increased international transactions and new global markets promoted efficiency (IMF Staff, 2008; Berkup, 2014). Generation X followed in the footsteps of the Baby Boomers, utilizing technology in their homes and throughout their daily lives. The individuals of this generation witnessed the invention of on-demand programming, cable, digital socialization, and digital entertainment such as video games. Generation X truly began to adopt technology into all aspects of their lives, doing so in an effort to streamline tasks to increase their time efficiency. Advances in a wide range of technical and scientific fields and industries led to translational developments that made their way into the medical field resulting in revolutionary devices such as computerized axial tomography (CAT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scanners (Patel and De Jesus, 2022; Filler, 2009). Healthcare stayed at the forefront for this generation, as individuals began to focus more and more on their own personal health and wellness coincident with having an increasing number of tools available to do so. Access to education continued to increase during this period, with the implementation of new federal policies, limiting segregation and creating enhanced access across socioeconomic groups and for the disabled. As a net effect individuals from Generation X are generally engaged in their healthcare, though, are less likely to utilize a single healthcare provider for their needs (Integrated Healthcare Executive, 2016). This generation generally believes healthcare providers are knowledgeable as well as reliable healthcare resources for information and care (Integrated Healthcare Executive, 2016). This generation also generally utilizes and responds to multiple forms of communication with health providers, i.e., verbal, written and online (Integrated Healthcare Executive, 2016).4.02.2.5 Generation Y (1981–1996)—The MillennialsMillennials are those born between 1981 and 1996, currently ages 26–41. These individuals were shaped by digital communication technologies and are known for their intrinsic desire for a sense of communal, democratic innovation where one is always expected to share new ideas and work as a team player (Karr, 2021). Millenials were the first generation to be raised with smartphones, instant communication methods, and social networking. Due to the availability of technology and its integration as an “essential” part of daily life, Millennials have been groomed by technology, and technology has shaped their interactions. This generation largely trusts in the ability of technology to underpin and advance the workforce and relies on it for nearly every aspect of their lives.As of 2015, Millennials made up more than one quarter of the U.S. population, totaling 83.1 million individuals, exceeding all other generations, with Baby Boomers closely following at 75.4 million individuals (Commerce.gov, 2015). With such a large population, Millennials have the potential for providing major influence and imparting a lasting impact on the direction and evolution of our society. As patients, Millennials will influence the future of healthcare in new ways, as their use of online resources and telehealth is innate in their daily operative practice and continues to grow. This group generally believes that healthcare costs are too high and that third-party health payers or insurers have too much power (Vogenberg and Santilli, 2018). With that being said, Millennials do not readily depend on primary care providers, seeking healthcare advice online or via urgent care. A survey completed by the Employment Benefit Research Institute revealed that only 65% of Millennials had primary care providers, in comparison to 74% of Generation X and 82% of baby boomers (Employee Benefit Research Institution, 2020). As the oldest Millennials are now entering their early 40s it will be interesting to see how this may shift, as they too will require greater healthcare services.4.02.2.6 Generation Z (1997–2012)Generation Z is the youngest generation of individuals in our society that we examine in this chapter. Of all the generations discussed so far it is Gen Z that is most likely to rely on and be impacted by Social Media now and well into the future as this means of communication and information sharing continues to evolve.Read full chapterURL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780128240106000721Generations of Users: DefinitionsIt should be noted that only user generations that are currently possible library patrons are considered here. Thus the user generations, as reported in the relevant literature, are defined as: (1) Baby Boomers; (2) Generation X; (3) the Millennial Generation or Generation Y; (4) Generation Z; and finally (5) Generation α (see Table 15.1).Table 15.1. Date of birth categorisation of user generationsUser generationAge in 2014Age spanBaby Boomer49–711943–1965Generation X49–331965–1981Millennial Generation35–241979–1990Generation Z24–41990–2010Generation α42010 – onwardsDate of birth could be considered as the definitive criterion in defining the different user generations. However, in the literature, there is a controversy regarding the age span of each user generation. With regard to Baby Boomers, Evandrou (1997) argued that these were born between 1946 and 1965, whereas Huber and Skidmore (2003) proposed a slightly different timeframe, starting in 1945 and ending in 1965. Radford and Connaway (2007, 2008) and Robbins (2012) defined Baby Boomers as those born between 1946 and 1964. However, Pankl (2004) provided a broader timeframe, suggesting that Baby Boomers were born anywhere between 1943 and 1946 and ending between 1960 and 1965. It could be argued that users born between 1943 and 1965 are considered Baby Boomers (see Table 15.1). They are also known as the ‘pig in the python’ group, because of their great effect on culture (Bailey, 2013).Generation X users follow Baby Boomers. Users born between 1965 and 1981 belong to Generation X (Kipnis and Childs, 2004; Somerville and Brar, 2006). There seems to be a common acceptance of the dates for this generation (see Table 15.1). However, the same cannot be said for the Millennial Generation. Kipnis and Childs (2004) argued that the Millennial Generation consists of users born between 1982 and 2004, whereas Sweeney (2005) proposed 1979 as the starting and 1994 as the ending dates for the Millennials. Wheeler and Harris (2006) argued that Millennials were born between 1982 and 2002. Corrado (2008) defines Millennials as those born between 1979 and 2000. Whatever the challenges in defining the date of birth for this generation, Millennials are the second in terms of numbers after the Baby Boomers (Konata, 2009; Makori, 2010) (see Table 15.1).There is not only a variety of different opinions regarding the specific date of birth for this generation but also a variety of different names referring to Millennials. The term Millennials is used interchangeably with Generation Y or Gen Y, the Net Generation, the Internet Generation, Echo Boomers, Boomlets, Nexters, the Nintendo Generation, the Digital Generation, the Sunshine Generation, Screenagers, the C Generation, the iGeneration, Generation Media, Generation MySpace among others (Connaway and Radford, 2007; Hebert and Wolk, 2008; Mercun and Žumer, 2008; Moulaison, 2008; Radford and Connaway, 2008; Switzer, 2008; Thomas and McDonald, 2005; Williams and Rowlands, 2007). The reasons for this variety of names are not known. However, we speculate that they are somehow related to the fact that Millenials comprise a large number of users and thus the range of labels demonstrates a variety of characteristics and a spectrum of sub-generations.Generation Z consists of all those born from 1990 to 2010 according to Sieberhagen (Sieberhagen, 2011), though Lee (2011) disagrees on the start date, proposing instead 1993. The overlap between the Millennial Generation and Generation Z may be attributable to the variety of characteristics these two generations share. Generation Z is widely accepted but terms such as ‘netgeners’, ‘screenagers’, ‘digital natives’ and ‘Google’ generation are also used to refer to the same users (Schmidt and Cribb, 2011). A new generation, the so-called Generation α, is now appearing. Specifically, Schmidt and Cribb (2011) argued that all users born from 2010 and onwards are members of Generation α (see Table 15.1).The proposed dates of births provide library and information professionals with a first insight into the ages and generations of the users whom they serve. Knowing the specific characteristics of each of these user generations is of considerable importance for developing and delivering information services successfully.Read full chapterURL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B97800810025130001591 IntroductionSociologists and researchers have studied five generational trends categorized as traditionalists, baby boomers, generation X, millennials and generation Z (Gen Z) (Poláková and Klímová, 2019). Students from each generation possess specific and unique characteristics due to the circumstances they grew up in (e.g. economic, social and cultural conditions) and these characteristics affect their perception of formal learning (Chicca and Shellenbarger 2018; Poláková and Klímová, 2019). For instance, the traditionalists (1925–1945), commonly known as the “silent generation”, were raised during wartime hence they respect authority and prefer to work in the background and favour instructor-driven lessons (i.e. structured and predictable classes (Cook and Macaulay, 2017; Wiedmer, 2015). For the baby boomers (1946–1964), they are workaholics who work extremely long hours under pressure, and they are collectivists who enjoy a democratic learning environment but also like learning new skills independently (Levonius, 2015; Poláková and Klímová, 2019). As for the generation X (1965–1980), learners are independent, self-directed, tech-savvy, open-minded and comfortable with authority (Levonius, 2015; Lissitsa and Kol, 2016). Currently, millennials (1981–1994) form the main bulk of students in higher education thus making them the most educated generation in history (Cilliers, 2017; Shatto and Erwin 2017). They are the most connected generation, the first generation to have computers in schools, are comfortable with using network learning and e-learning and prefer participatory, activity-based group work and enjoy collaboration with peers in the classroom setting (Cook and Macaulay, 2017). With distinct learning styles and preferences, no panacea is able to accommodate the learning needs of all the generations hence it is essential to update the educational framework and pedagogy to meet each generation’s learning needs (Rothman, 2016; Shatto and Erwin, 2016).The latest generation, widely known as Gen Z, iGen, iGeneration, digital natives, home landers or post-millennials, has been defined with varying age demographics as, Pew Research Center defines Gen Z as anyone born from 1997 onward (Dimock, 2019) while other literature sources indicate that they are born from 1995 to present (Hampton and Keys, 2017; Lines and Metcalf, 2017; Chicca and Shellenbarger 2018; Hampton et al., 2020; Seemiller and Grace, 2016). Hence, in this review we define anyone born from 1995 onward as part of Gen Z (Oducado, 2019).Gen Z is the youngest generation of students to attend school (Dimock, 2019). This generation of students is like millennials as they have an increased exposure to technology in education and both generations are characterised by their receptiveness to using technology and ability to multitask (Black, 2010; Szymkowiak et al., 2021). Despite these similarities, there are generational differences between the Gen Z and millennial students in terms of learning styles, preferences, communication, preferred type of feedback, extent of technology use, online social connectedness and the ways they view risk taking (Issacs et al., 2020; Twenge, 2017). Millennials are tech-savvy, prefer a collaborative learning style with blended learning and have effective in-person and online communication skills (Issacs et al., 2020). They desire constructive and immediate feedback, are highly connected on social media and are idealistic risk-takers (Issacs et al., 2020; Chicca and Shellenbarger, 2018). On the other hand, Gen Z students are digital natives who prefer an independent learning style with less passive but more visual and kinaesthetic learning. They also desire convenience and are open to honest feedback (Issacs et al., 2020). Due to the extensive reliance on technology, Gen Z students have underdeveloped in-person social skills as they lack in the nuances and art of conversation and this lack of face to-face communication skills will potentially inhibit their development of skills to connect socially and in person with patients as healthcare professionals (Seemiller and Grace, 2016; Chicca and Shellenbarger, 2018; Turner, 2015). Despite being highly connected on social media, they value privacy and are pragmatic and entrepreneurial (Issacs et al., 2020; Chicca and Shellenbarger 2018). They are more risk averse compared with the millennials as many of them have grown up during the period of economic recession (Chicca and Shellenbarger 2018). The similar yet distinct characteristics of the millennials and Gen Z have necessitated the need for educators to alter educational practices, pedagogies and teaching approach to provide an optimal and holistic learning environment that meets their learning needs.The few studies and reviews on Gen Z in the literature have focused on topics such as their characteristics (Dimock, 2019; Howe and Strauss, 2000; Seemiller and Grace, 2016; Twenge, 2017), effective strategies to recruit and retain them in public sector (Acheampong, 2019) and the main characteristics that would attract them to join brick-and-mortar retail settings (Vojvodić, 2019,2018). A critical review of the work-related attitudes of the Gen Z in China (Tang, 2019) and their use of social media and its repercussions at the individual, organisational and societal levels have been explored (Prakash Yadav and Rai, 2017). Recently, Martin et al. (2020) conducted a systematic review of emerging learning environment and technology used in education such as mobile learning, special education technology, massive open online courses and social media (Martin et al., 2020). However, the focus was not specific to Gen Z healthcare students and their learning styles, preferences and needs. Given the dearth of research on Gen Z healthcare students and their specific learning needs, views and learning experiences, it is imperative to consolidate evidence on this topic to facilitate teaching and to drive future research and educational practices.According to Arksey and O'Malley (2005), the purpose of a scoping review is to form a summative map of available evidence and to identify research gaps and hence, we deemed it as the most appropriate methodology to address the heterogenous and emerging Gen Z healthcare literature.Read full articleURL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S14715953210028335.1 Viewership across demographicsConsumer culture is influenced by four generations: Baby Boomers, Generation X, Generation Y (or Millennials), and Generation Z (or Centennials). During the past decade, we have seen TV evolve from traditional linear broadcast networks, cable networks, and syndicated selections to streaming services, over-the-top (OTT), and connected TV. The following section discusses the influence of OTT on the four generations. Niosi (2021) classified the generations like Baby Boomers: born between 1946 and 1964, Generation X: born between 1965 and 1981, Generation Y (millennials): born between 1982 and 1997, and Generation Z (Digital Natives or Centennials): born between 1997 and today.In order to understand viewership across generations X, Y, and Z, it is important to take a more nuanced approach. In terms of audience age groups, Nielsen data showed a sharp decline in viewing traditional TV by younger audiences. Centennials and Millennials are watching 40% fewer traditional TV shows than they did 5 years ago, and the time spent watching traditional TV has decreased by 25%. In fact, this decline is not only affecting the younger audience - according to Nielsen's Total Audience Report, traditional TV watching has decreased by 13% among Gen Xers as well, while it has remained relatively flat among adults aged 50–64. On the contrary, Baby Boomers actually increased traditional TV watch time by over 7% in the past five years, showing linear TV viewing slowed down with age (Nielsen, 2021).According to Massad (2018), the research literature on OTT is largely dominated by the theme that it was born out of a generational shift in viewing habits. For instance, Generation Z and Millennials preferred the ad-free model they grew up with, while Boomers and Matures preferred the subscription model they grew up with. Additionally, advertisement tolerance ranges between seven and fourteen minutes per hour for all consumers (Westcott et al., 2019; Westcott, 2019).Read full articleURL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0736585322000302ConclusionDefining user generations is not an easy task. Each user generation has its own unique characteristics which are informed by a variety of social, economic and technological factors. However, we have been able to identify some common characteristics among user generations, for example the Millennial Generation and Generation Z. These characteristics can be valuable for public libraries that offer information services to a wide range of age groups. Knowing the specific characteristics of each user generation is important for libraries and librarians when they are called to formulate their policy on offering information services. In addition, knowing the specific factors that led to the development of these characteristics can assist librarians in making informed decisions regarding the future format of information resources, services and libraries in general. Libraries of any type have a great challenge to face: that of finding out how different user generations will interact with the same resources, share the same information and use the same information services. It seems that libraries can meet this challenge by embracing new technologies and offering information literacy programmes to their users.Read full chapterURL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780081002513000159Millennials are differentTechnology has moved beyond work and entertainment into the area of social interaction. Economics, technology and social factors all play a role in creating the variations that distinguish one generation from another. Although there is overlap between the birth dates associated with each generation, it is the similarities among individuals born in a specific age range that make them different from those who come before and after.The six named generations are: the Greatest Generation, the Silent Generation, the Baby Boomers, Generation X, Generation Y and Generation Z. The Greatest Generation is composed of people who matured during the Depression and fought in World War II. Members of the Silent Generation, too young to fight in World War II, were influenced by childhood experiences of the Depression. The Baby Boomer generation grew up during the time of affluence after the war, and as teenagers engaged in an antiestablishment counter-culture. They were followed by Generation X, which was raised in two-income families, creating an independent and resourceful generation suspicious of authority. Generation Y, also known as the Millennial Generation, is now coming into adulthood and these young people are the first generation to grow to maturity having never experienced a world without computers. The ubiquitous presence of electronic gadgets has profoundly influenced this generation to the extent they have been called digital natives because of their ability to understand and manipulate technology in an organic way that is unfamiliar to older generations. The Millennials are followed by Generation Z, also called the Internet Generation because of their early exposure to the Internet and the convenience delivered through networks.Beginning with the Millennial Generation the number of years between generations appears to be growing smaller (see Table 2.1). Some factor is, or some factors are, influencing people so dramatically as to create differences that are reducing the time between generations. This trend seems to match the increasing speed of technology penetration within society, so it is not surprising that the Millennial Generation is taking the lead in a cultural revolution that includes technology. This generation uses technology whenever and wherever they want and they are as likely to send a text message at 2.00 a.m. as 2.00 p.m. They blend work, home and social lives into a seamless continuum, and technology is the glue that holds it together. They reject traditional classrooms and don't like being cooped up in an office. They also want to be judged on their performance, not on predictable office hours (Tapscott, 2009). They are comfortable figuring out new technology and love customizing their gadgets with wallpapers, ring tones and apps to notify them of updates from social media sites. Social networking enables this generation to collaborate in a manner that keeps them connected 24 hours a day. They collaborate through chat rooms, blogs, instant messaging and multi-user games, and they share everything from personal insights to challenges at work.Table 2.1. Generational timelineGenerationBirth date rangeNumber of yearsGreatest Generation1901192423Silent Generation1925194520Baby Boomers1946196418Generation X1961198019Millennial198119898Generation Z199019999As confident as Millennials are in their technology culture, there are hidden dangers in their openness. Notifications come at all times of the day and night, and can be seen by others as interruptions. Living in a technology culture that is always on can result in a loss of freedom because of expectations that a person will always respond immediately. Further, there is nowhere to hide when technology is constantly updating a person's GPS location, turning privacy into an illusion. Privacy is a concern that deters many older generations from embracing the technology culture. They are worried about the amount of personal information available to the public and about how it is being used. E-book vendors are collecting a large amount of information on their users; everything from the average length of time it takes to read a book to how people browse is being collected without the knowledge of readers (Alter, 2012: 1). Although much of this information is gathered in order to analyze use for future publications, librarians see this data as an intrusion into personal space.Older generations which have adopted aspects of this culture have not integrated information technology into their “DNA” as the Millennials seem to have done. Neurobiologists are just beginning to explore the effects early exposure to technology is having on brain development (Prensky, 2001). An experiment was undertaken by Gary Small using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to determine whether prior experience with technology influenced brain function. Those with prior experience of searching the web activated different parts of the brain than those with no experience. This experiment involved a small sample of 24 subjects aged 55–78, and “despite such limitations, our findings point to an association between routine Internet searching and neural circuitry activation in middle-aged and older adults”(Small et al., 2009: 125).It will be interesting to see if this experiment can be replicated, but the possibility that exposure to instant answers and web search results is altering brain functions is startling. If our thought patterns are being modified by experience with technology as is suggested, then it is important to understand those changes. For example, Baby Boomers experienced the growth of television, whereas Generation X experienced the computer revolution, Millennials have experienced rapid internet expansion, and Generation Z has experienced the benefits of all of the above and the emergence and explosion of social media (Dimock, 2019). As generations have aged, each generation has had more integration of technology and digital devices into their lives. Prensky has introduced the terms “digital natives” and “digital immigrants” to separate generations who have grown up with technology from those who have not (2001). These experiences with technology and its perceived intuitiveness informs each generations’ views of technology and its place in their lives. Although individual views and utilization of technology may vary within a generation, there are broad generalizations that can be made with regards to the views and adoption of digital devices and the internet for social interaction based on an individual's age. Ball, 2019; Woodford, 2022; Yuko, 2022). While one generation learned how to utilize their associated technologies during their formative years, the subsequent generation was faced with even more advanced technologies thus diminishing the learning curve and knowledge gap from generation to generation and introducing technologies at earlier ages. In the case of the Baby Boomer generation, significant advancements were made during the formative years; however, much of these innovations were targeted at large-scale companies and militaristic needs rather than targeting the individual consumer level as is especially seen in the later generations, particularly Generation Z.Younger generations tend to have more positive views on technology and its integration into society and social interaction as they have experienced technology since birth (Vogels, 2019; Van Volkom et al., 2014). Younger generations, including Generations X, Y and Z, are more likely to utilize digital devices on a daily basis for personal, professional, and educational purposes (Prensky, 2001; Vogels, 2019). For example, a large majority of the individuals belonging to these three generations own smartphones and use social media regularly (Vogels, 2019). Nearly all of those who belong to these younger generations utilize the internet to some degree, either via smartphone or other digital devices (Vogels, 2019). The younger generational cohorts, including Generations Y and Z, have experienced the integration of technology into their education, making technology a fundamental part of their learning experiences and lives (Prensky, 2001). These interactions with technology and digital devices since childhood have created the pattern of reliance on technology for social interaction and integration into all aspects of life, both personal and professional.Older generations who are considered “digital immigrants,” tend to have less positive views about the digitization of the world and thus have lower utilization rates of technology and the internet. Baby Boomers and older generations utilize smartphones and social media to a lesser degree, with Baby Boomers having higher rates of utilization than older generations (Vogels, 2019). This variable technology use also scales with use of the internet and positive views of the internet on society, with the silent generation having the lowest rates utilization and positive perspectives on the internet (Vogels, 2019). Older adults were less likely to report that technology has altered the way in which they socially interact with others (Van Volkom et al., 2014). Older generations tend to report that technology has decreased human interaction (Van Volkom et al., 2014; Heinz et al., 2013). However, while technology continues to advance and become an essential part of daily life, older generations have adopted newer technologies in some form or another at a faster rate than before (Vogels, 2019). These characteristics have previously been reported in the literature which highlighted Gen Z students’ inclination to learn in an environment where they could actively participate and learn independently, engage in hands-on activities and use their aural, visual and kinaesthetic senses (Barnes and Noble College, 2018; Keeley et al., 2015; Loveland, 2017; Seemiller and Grace, 2016; Spears et al., 2015; Turner, 2015). These learning styles align with the other generations of students (i.e., generation X and millennials) (Dimock, 2019; Seemiller and Grace, 2016; Poláková and Klímová, 2019; Twenge, 2017) and were demonstrated through their learning preferences and needs, where they preferred self-paced learning and an engaging learning environment which is heavily influenced by technology (e.g. using videos, simulations, online quizzes, case studies and social media). Recent studies which examined technology integration in Gen Z classrooms have demonstrated positive outcomes in students’ achievements and an overall acceptance and positive perception of digital learning and communication and will also meet the learning styles, preferences and the needs of this generation of healthcare students (Li et al., 2018; Oducado 2019; Poláková and Klímová, 2019). Previous research has demonstrated that the integration of technology in education is effective, meaningful and necessary to keep up with technology trends and today’s learners (Dania et al., 2011; Ghavifekr and Rosdy, 2015; Sööt, 2013). Furthermore, existing reviews have reported the use of social media in education as a novel tool to support learning and improve communication and social skills (Kakushi and Évora, 2016; Price et al., 2018; Ross and Myers, 2017; Wahila et al., 2018). In addition, a recent qualitative study examining nursing students’ and clinical facilitators’ experiences with patient training using virtual reality simulations of case scenarios demonstrated an improvement in students’ communication skills (Author, XXXX). Students and facilitators also recognized the benefits and the potential of using the simulations; however, concerns about the lack of authenticity were raised (Author, XXXX). The limited studies examining technology integration specific to Gen Z healthcare students propels for further studies to examine and confirm the effectiveness of various technology integration on Gen Z healthcare students’ overall learning in the classroom and their communication skills. Essentially, educators and relevant stakeholders could plan carefully before integrating technology in classrooms to ensure that the undertaking will be safe, secured and relevant for Gen Z healthcare students and other generations of students with similar learning styles and preferences, without it detracting from the content of instruction (Oducado 2019; Cordoş et al. 2019).The Gen Z healthcare students highlighted the need for immediate and constructive feedback from educators and wished for educators to assist them in their overall development and prepare them for their future career. These preferences and needs align with Gen Z’s attributes where they desire instant gratification and are pragmatic individuals who are concerned about their future. The literature also reported that akin to the millennials, Gen Z are multitaskers who lack patience, prefer quantity of information rather than quality and expect prompt feedback (Mohr and Mohr, 2017; Seemiller and Grace, 2016; Twenge, 2017). Furthermore, the pragmatic nature of Gen X, Gen Y and in this case, Gen Z healthcare students could be attributed to the circumstances they grew up in — a period of public violence and economic uncertainty (Loveland, 2017; Shatto & Erwin 2016; Chicca and Shellenbarger 2018). As such, they become individuals who worry excessively and are less likely to take risks compared with previous generations (Seemiller and Grace, 2016; Turner, 2015). They also wish to have educators who can reassure them and prepare them for their future career. Storytelling was highlighted as a plausible approach to teach healthcare students. To stay updated, technology and storytelling can be combined — digital storytelling has shown effectiveness in engaging students for deep and meaningful learning and even in nurse education (i.e. patient case studies) (Christiansen, 2011; Smeda et al., 2014). Educators could integrate storytelling and story living activities to resonate with students and share their experiences as practitioners and educators thus allowing students to be prepared and subsequently boost their confidence for their future career. Hence, future studies could focus on training educators to adopt and integrate digital storytelling and examine the association between digital storytelling and Gen Z healthcare students’ perceived confidence about their future.The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic has and will continue to have a substantial effect on education, especially for the healthcare students who have been pushed to mostly online curriculum and reduced clinical exposure (Marshall and Wolanskyj-Spinner, 2020). Therefore, technological incorporation in learning content as well as in enhancing clinical skills via virtual reality stimulations could potentially be a small step in the right direction in the ever-evolving academic arena (Author, XXXX).The future directions and recommendations for educators teaching Gen Z students include the adoption of a theoretical framework that could be integrated to inform the development and delivery of teaching-learning approaches and to explore the underlying mechanisms that could affect the outcome (Health et al., 2015). This coupled with the framework by Brinthaupt et al. (2011), which highlights the 3 broad categories namely fostering student engagement, stimulating intellectual development and building rapport with students (Brinthaupt et al., 2011), could be considered in guiding the teaching-learning approaches for educators to address the digital learning needs of the Gen Z students when designing future pedagogy. It is of paramount importance for educators and stakeholders to be aware of, as well as to plan, facilitate and prevent the possibility of drawbacks of technology dominance (e.g. decreased overall well-being) and this can be done by the faculty members, peer mentors and specialists such as counsellors providing support to the students (Chicca and Shellenbarger 2018; Oducado 2019). Whilst technology is a major component of Gen Z student’s learning, blended learning has proven to improve the learning outcome for theoretical knowledge to a greater level than either face-to-face learning or e-learning alone (Bock et al., 2021).In view of the increased psychological vulnerability of Gen Z students (Demirci et al., 2019) given their poorer mental health status (Twenge et al., 2018, 2019) coupled with mental health being of an increased priority for them, a comprehensive framework which may include mental health screening whereby teachers as well as students are educated on potential risk factors and signs and symptoms to look out for, counselling services in school is the cogent way forward (Adelman and Taylor, 2006). Additionally, a list of resources specifying helplines for mental health matters could be provided for all students to maintain their overall well-being (Chunta et al., 2020;2021; Oducado 2019).4.1 LimitationsBecause of the inclusion of only studies published in English, unclear titles and abstracts, poor indexing and exclusion of studies with an overview of Gen Z, relevant studies may have been missed out. Most of the studies were Western-based and whilst the other studies were geographically well-distributed, the sparsity of studies included from the other regions implies the necessity for further inclusion of geographically and culturally distributed studies and reviews that focus on students’ learning preferences and needs. Additionally, the included research reports were quantitatively designed (n = 7) and due to the lack of a quality appraisal of the included studies, the quantity of data generated is limited and may not capture ample information that addresses the research question of this review. Other included articles are perspectives, commentary or editorial and therefore, consideration of potential bias in these articles may require further examination. Furthermore, because of the nature of a scoping review, the focus was on the breadth (to cover all available evidence) compared with the depth (provision of detailed analysis and appraisal of the quality of the included studies) that may further limit the transferability of the evidence. As Gen Z-related research is an emerging topic, mixed-methods or qualitative research studies and systematic reviews could be adopted to capture more data to develop specific insights and understand students’ attitudes and learning experiences using a fluid approach. Despite the inclusion of studies from four different healthcare disciplines (i.e. nursing, medicine, psychology and pharmaceutical science), no differences between the students’ learning styles, preferences and needs were highlighted. This implies the need for future studies to examine the specific preferences and needs of healthcare disciplines and educational subjects (e.g. languages). Furthermore, due to the heterogeneity of the included studies, there could have been an overemphasis on the gaps that need to be addressed in the literature. Finally, Arksey, O'Malley (2005) recommend a further optional step of undertaking stakeholder consultation to augment a review’s findings, however this step was not undertaken given time and resource constraints but could well have served to enhance the comprehensiveness of this review.Despite these limitations, this review has broadened the current literature by consolidating and providing a better insight and a reiteration of Gen Z healthcare students’ learning styles, preferences and needs and how these needs can be met.4.2 Implications for health practice and health policyMore geographically and culturally diverse studies which examine the effectiveness of technology integration and digital storytelling to boost students’ learning and confidence in their future career need to be performed, especially given the rapidly changing situation given the Covid-19 pandemic. However, these integrations must be carefully planned, alongside campus resources and self-care strategies, to ensure an optimal and safe learning environment. More Gen Z-related studies that adopt the mixed-methods and qualitative design are needed to capture in-depth and comprehensive insights about this generation and whether their preferences and needs are discipline- or subject- specific. The specific preferences and needs of the unique healthcare disciplines and educational subjects should be examined.
